title: Registration and device-enrollment data can be linked to a specific household profile
description: The Home Hub receives account-registration details together with camera/sensor enrollment information on the same flow. If identifiers such as email, username, device serial numbers, MAC addresses, or installation metadata are combined, the hub or downstream services can link multiple devices and actions to the same homeowner/household, enabling profiling of occupancy, device ownership, and behavior.
assumptions: The registration/enrollment flow contains persistent account identifiers and device identifiers or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context confirms L applies to ExternalEntity->Process flows but does not provide a more specific subtree citation.

title: Enrollment data may identify the homeowner directly or indirectly
description: Account registration commonly includes directly identifying data such as name, email, phone number, address, or billing details. Even if direct identifiers are minimized, enrolled device identifiers and home-installation context can indirectly identify the homeowner or household when associated with a residence.
assumptions: The flow includes account details and device metadata sufficient to identify a person or household.
uncertainty_note: Specific subtree id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only establishes applicability of Identifiability to this flow type.

title: Registration and enrollment reveal sensitive home setup information
description: The flow may disclose the presence, type, number, and placement context of cameras and sensors in the home. This can reveal private facts about the household, such as security posture, room usage, occupancy patterns, or the presence of children, elderly residents, or special monitoring needs.
assumptions: Enrollment includes device types, names, locations, or configuration metadata beyond a bare device count.
uncertainty_note: Applies if enrollment metadata includes meaningful device/context details; if only opaque device tokens are sent, disclosure risk is lower.

title: The homeowner may be unaware of the extent of personal data collected during onboarding
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the Home Hub may collect more data than the homeowner expects, such as device identifiers, network information, location/timezone, household composition hints, or telemetry needed for setup. If notices are incomplete or unclear, the user may not detect what personal data is being processed.
assumptions: The onboarding UX does not fully and clearly explain all categories of personal data collected and their purposes.
uncertainty_note: Threat is grounded in typical onboarding opacity; exact applicability depends on the transparency of the registration/enrollment interface.

title: The homeowner may not understand privacy implications of enrolling cameras and sensors
description: The consequences of enrolling monitoring devices may be insufficiently understandable to the homeowner, especially regarding what data each device will later collect, who can access it, retention periods, and whether household members or visitors are affected. This undermines informed decision-making at setup time.
assumptions: The setup flow does not present privacy-relevant explanations in a clear, timely, and comprehensible way.
uncertainty_note: Specific subtree id selected by best judgement; context supports Unawareness on this interaction type but not a finer-grained node.

title: Account registration and device enrollment may occur without valid or sufficiently specific consent/legal basis
description: If the Home Hub collects personal data for account creation and device onboarding without obtaining valid consent where required, or without another appropriate legal basis and clear purpose specification, the processing may be non-compliant. This is especially relevant if data from cameras/sensors or household metadata are collected by default during setup.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires consent or another explicit legal basis for some onboarding data processing activities.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and deployment model; this is a genuine risk but legal applicability may vary.

title: Temporary access code can identify or single out a guest
description: The temporary access code entered by the guest may function as a unique token tied to a specific guest invitation, booking, or visit window. When Home Hub receives the code, it can identify or single out that guest and link the unlock attempt to that person or household visit.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary code is unique per guest, stay, or visit and that Home Hub or connected services log code use.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the specific identifiability subtree.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having used the temporary code
description: If Home Hub records the submitted temporary code together with timestamp and door-unlock event, the resulting evidence may be used to prove that a particular guest accessed the property. This can reduce the guest's plausible deniability regarding presence or entry.
assumptions: Assumes access attempts are logged and codes are attributable to a specific guest or invitation.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-repudiation subtree id not present in retrieved context; node selection is approximate.

title: Disclosure of the temporary access code during entry
description: The temporary access code is privacy-relevant authentication data. If the code is transmitted, processed, or logged insecurely by Home Hub, unauthorized parties could learn the code and infer the guest's authorized access window or presence.
assumptions: Assumes the code is visible in transit within the device/software boundary, stored in logs, or otherwise accessible to unauthorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies generally to this flow, but exact disclosure path depends on implementation details not provided.

title: Guest may be unaware they are sharing personal data when entering the code
description: When entering a temporary access code at Home Hub, the guest may not realize that the code submission can be treated as personal data about their visit, presence, and access event, and may be logged or further processed.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform guests about logging, retention, or downstream use of access events.

title: Guest code processing may lack a valid legal basis or exceed purpose limitation
description: Processing the temporary access code and associated access event may be non-compliant if the system collects more data than necessary, retains it too long, or uses it for purposes beyond granting temporary entry, without an appropriate legal basis or adequate notice.
assumptions: Assumes personal data law applies and that access-code events are stored or reused beyond immediate authentication.

title: Event log enables linkage of household activity over time
description: Writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a single local event log creates a consolidated history that can be linked across timestamps, sensors, and rooms/devices. This can reveal routines, occupancy patterns, and relationships between events that identify or single out household members.
assumptions: The local event log stores multiple event types with timestamps and retains them long enough for correlation.

title: Logged sensor events may identify residents through behavior patterns
description: Even if the log does not contain explicit names, repeated motion/door/sensor events with timestamps can identify a household or particular resident by their distinctive daily routines, presence patterns, sleep/wake cycles, or room usage.
assumptions: Event records are associated with a specific home and contain sufficiently granular timestamps or sensor identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subtree id is approximate; applicability of identifiability is strong but depends on event granularity and household context.

description: The act of writing sensor events to the local log makes residents' activities detectable within the system. Motion and door events directly expose when someone is present, moving, entering, leaving, or inactive, enabling inference of occupancy and habits.

title: Excessive disclosure through detailed local event logging

Fine-grained timestamps and raw event histories can reveal intimate household routines, occupancy, and behavior beyond what is strictly required.
assumptions: Not all raw events or their full retention period are necessary for the intended functionality.

title: Residents may be unaware that in-home activities are persistently logged
description: If the Home Hub silently writes motion, door, and sensor events to a local event log, residents or visitors may not understand that their in-home activities are being recorded and retained. This undermines transparency about what data is processed and for what purpose.
assumptions: The system does not clearly notify users and visitors about local logging, retention, and use of event histories.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; applicability depends on whether transparency notices are provided elsewhere in the system.

title: Logging household sensor events may occur without valid consent or other legal basis
description: Motion, door, and sensor events can constitute personal data about residents and visitors. Persistently storing these events in the local log may be non-compliant if the system lacks a valid legal basis, fails to honor consent preferences, or retains data longer than permitted.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires a legal basis, purpose limitation, and retention controls for this category of household activity data.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, deployment context, and whether another legal basis besides consent applies.

title: Sensitive video clips may be disclosed during upload to cloud storage

description: Residents, guests, or passers-by captured by the cameras may not understand that recordings are not only captured locally but also uploaded to a remote cloud datastore. This lack of awareness undermines transparency about where personal data goes and how it is processed.

This can hinder accountability and dispute resolution around personal data handling.

description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than necessary in the motion alert to the backend, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, location/room labels, or rich sensor context, when only a minimal event signal is needed. This would disclose avoidable personal data about occupants' presence and behavior.
assumptions: The motion alert contains personal data or metadata related to household occupancy or behavior, and the backend does not strictly require all included fields for its purpose.

title: Linkability via persistent hub or household identifiers in alerts
description: If each motion alert includes stable identifiers for the hub, household, sensor, or account, the backend can link multiple alerts over time and build a detailed activity pattern for the same home. This enables correlation of events into occupancy routines and behavioral profiles beyond the immediate alerting purpose.

title: Identifiability of residents from motion alert metadata
description: Even if the alert does not contain direct names, metadata such as hub ID, account reference, address-linked device registration, or room-specific sensor labels may allow the backend to identify the household or infer which resident triggered the event. Real-time motion events are strongly tied to individuals' presence in the home.
assumptions: Backend operators or connected systems can resolve device/account metadata to a specific household or person.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best-effort; identifiability depends on whether the backend can map alert metadata to a person or household.

title: Detectability of in-home activity from incoming alert traffic
description: The backend can detect when motion occurs in the home simply from receiving the alert flow, even before inspecting full content. Timing, frequency, and presence of alerts reveal occupancy and activity patterns, making the occurrence of a privacy-sensitive event observable.
assumptions: The mere arrival, timing, or volume of alerts is observable at the backend or by components with access to backend ingress telemetry.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is inferred; threat is grounded in detectability from event occurrence and metadata rather than payload content alone.

title: Processing of motion alerts beyond user expectations or consent

This creates a non-compliance risk if purpose limitation, transparency, or consent requirements are not met.
assumptions: The system may repurpose or retain motion alert data beyond the immediate notification function, and applicable privacy requirements constrain such use.

description: The backend may include more personal data than necessary in the push notification payload or visible notification text, such as exact timestamps, camera/location identifiers, thumbnails, or occupancy-related details. Because notifications are delivered across platform push services and may appear on a locked screen, this can disclose the homeowner's presence patterns or household activity beyond what is strictly needed to alert them.

title: Repeated motion alerts enable inference of homeowner routines
description: Even if each notification is individually minimal, the pattern, timing, and frequency of motion-detected notifications sent to the homeowner can reveal occupancy schedules, sleep/work routines, travel periods, or other behavioral patterns. An observer of the device or an intermediary handling notification metadata could infer sensitive household habits.
assumptions: Notification timing/frequency is observable by someone other than the intended recipient, such as a shoulder-surfer, family member, employer-managed device administrator, or push-service intermediary.
uncertainty_note: Exact inferenceability subnode is a best-fit estimate; applicability depends on whether notification metadata/timing is exposed outside the trusted context.

title: Notification content may be used for a purpose not expected by the homeowner
description: If motion-event notification data is reused by the backend or notification ecosystem for analytics, engagement optimization, profiling, or cross-feature personalization, the flow can support secondary use beyond the homeowner's expectation of receiving a security alert. This creates an unlinkability risk because event data becomes associated with broader user profiles or other contexts.
assumptions: The service or integrated notification/analytics components process event-notification data for secondary purposes beyond immediate alert delivery.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on backend or third-party reuse not stated in the flow description; included as a plausible genuine risk only if such secondary processing exists.

title: Motion notifications may be sent without sufficiently informed consent or user control
description: If the homeowner has not been clearly informed about what motion-event data will be included in notifications, when alerts will be sent, and through which channels or intermediaries, the notification flow may not meet consent and transparency expectations. Lack of granular controls over lock-screen visibility, rich media, or alert categories can further undermine valid consent.
assumptions: The system relies on consent or user choice for notification behavior and does not provide sufficiently specific notice or controls.
uncertainty_note: Consent/compliance applicability depends on the product's legal basis and UX; exact subnode is a best-fit estimate.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend may still transmit stable device, account, cohort, timestamp, or event-pattern attributes that allow the cloud analytics vendor to link multiple records to the same user, device, or household over time, especially when combined with the vendor's existing datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the aggregation is not fully anonymizing and that some persistent or quasi-identifying dimensions remain in the shared analytics payload or metadata.

title: Vendor may infer identities from aggregated analytics
description: The cloud analytics vendor may be able to identify a user, device, or small group from the received analytics by combining aggregates with auxiliary information such as IP ranges, customer account context, rare usage patterns, geography, or other datasets already held by the vendor.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has access to auxiliary data and that the aggregates are sufficiently granular to support singling out or re-identification.
uncertainty_note: Applies if aggregation granularity is high or cohorts are small; if strong anonymization and minimum-group thresholds are enforced, this threat may be reduced.

title: Analytics sharing may reveal sensitive usage behavior
description: Even without direct identifiers, aggregated device-usage analytics can disclose sensitive information about users or groups, such as health-related app usage, religious practices, sleep patterns, location routines, or other behavioral traits, when the vendor analyzes the received data.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics categories or dimensions reflect potentially sensitive behavior or special-category personal data.
uncertainty_note: Sensitivity depends on the actual telemetry fields and segmentation dimensions included in the shared analytics.

title: Users may be unaware that analytics are shared with a third-party vendor
description: If the mobile app backend sends analytics to an external cloud analytics vendor without clear, timely notice, users may not understand that a separate party receives and processes their usage data, nor the purposes and consequences of that sharing.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices, in-app disclosures, or just-in-time explanations are absent, unclear, or incomplete regarding third-party analytics sharing.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for third-party analytics integrations, but actual applicability depends on the app's transparency mechanisms.

title: Sharing analytics with the vendor may exceed consent or lawful-purpose boundaries
description: The backend may disclose device-usage analytics to the cloud analytics vendor for analytics, profiling, or secondary purposes that are not covered by the user's consent, legitimate expectations, contractual necessity, or other lawful basis, especially if the data is reused beyond service improvement.
assumptions: Assumes the organization has not established or enforced an appropriate legal basis, purpose limitation, data-processing agreement, or consent scope for this transfer.
uncertainty_note: Compliance conclusions are jurisdiction- and implementation-specific; this threat reflects plausible non-compliance risk rather than a confirmed violation.
